Q: ASP.NET MVC C# with SQL without ORM A:

As you mentioned, you can use "classic" SQL commands with ADO.NET. Here is a good example: Using ASP.Net MVC with Classic ADO.Net

Another way, and in my opinion a very fast and convenient way, is to use the Dapper framework. I would recommend you to use Dapper with Stored Procedures. It's a good trade-off between ORM (like Entity Framework) and classical SQL commands.

Q: T4 without Visual Studio A:

I wrote a cleanly reverse-engineered implementation of a T4 engine for the MonoDevelop IDE. It's open-source, licensed under the permissive MIT/X11 license, so you are free to embed the engine in your app or redistribute it. There's also an implementation of the TextTransform.exe command-line tool available as a dotnet global tool, and some APIs in the Mono.TextTemplating namespace to aid in hosting the engine.

You can get packages from NuGet and the source is on GitHub.

Q: Is there a built in function for string natural sort? A:

Solution 1: Question-specific, “fair enough” (but not generally suitable)

The built-in Python function str.zfill(width) returns a copy of the string left-filled with ASCII 0 digits to make a string of length width:

# inline implementation:
elms = ['Elm11', 'Elm12', 'Elm2', 'elm0', 'elm1', 'elm10', 'elm13', 'elm9']
max_str_len = max([len(s) for s in elms])
sorted(elms, key=lambda x: x.zfill(max_str_len + 1).casefold())

# same result using str.format() syntax:
sorted(elms, key=lambda x: '{:0>{width}}'.format(x, width=max_str_len + 1).casefold())

# as a function:
def ns_with_zfill(lst: list) -> list:
    max_str_len = max([len(s) for s in lst])
    return sorted(lst, key=lambda s: s.zfill(max_str_len + 1).casefold())

elms = ['Elm11', 'Elm12', 'Elm2', 'elm0', 'elm1', 'elm10', 'elm13', 'elm9']
ns_with_zfill(elms)

In both cases, the naturally sorted list returned is

['elm0', 'elm1', 'Elm2', 'elm9', 'elm10', 'Elm11', 'Elm12', 'elm13']

🚩 ⚠️ However, as it has been pointed out in the comments, the above solution actually has a weakness in that it doesn't work in general. For example it would put 'zlm1' before 'elm99' (since '00zlm1' < '0elm99'), so it's fair to say this solution actually fails to naturally sort strings with mixed prefixes:

elms = ['Elm11', 'Elm12', 'Elm2', 'elm0', 'elm1', 'elm10', 'elm13', 'elm9']
mixed = ['zlm1', 'elm99', 'alm5']
print(f'{ns_with_zfill(elms + mixed) = }')

❌ Result (it fails to sort correctly):

ns_with_zfill(elms + mixed) = ['alm5', 'elm0', 'elm1', 'Elm2', 'elm9', 'zlm1', 'elm10', 'Elm11', 'Elm12', 'elm13', 'elm99']

Solution 2: A better, universally resilient solution

A broader solution — still using only the built-in Python API, no third-party packages — may consist in splitting each string into its alphabetic and numeric components before comparison (ie split 'elm99' into ('elm', 99), 'zlm1' into ('zlm', 1), etc). The built-in Python function re.Pattern.split(string) (supposed to be faster than its close relative re.split(pattern, string)) does exactly that, provided that the regex pattern (a range of one or more digits), which here acts as a separator, is a group (ie is put in parentheses) so that the separator itself is kept too as part of the resulting list (which won't happen if you omit those parentheses, so you know):

import re

def ns_with_re_split(lst: list,
                     pattern_obj: re.Pattern = re.compile(r'(\d+)')
                     ) -> list:
    return sorted(lst, key=lambda s: [int(part) if part.isdigit() else part.casefold() for part in pattern_obj.split(s)])

elms = ['Elm11', 'Elm12', 'Elm2', 'elm0', 'elm1', 'elm10', 'elm13', 'elm9']
mixed = ['zlm1', 'elm99', 'alm5']
print(f'{ns_with_re_split(elms + mixed) = }')
ipv4s = ['10.0.0.2', '192.168.0.2', '192.168.0.4', '10.0.0.5', '192.168.0.12', '10.0.0.20']
print(f'{ns_with_re_split(ipv4s) = }')

✅ Result (it sorts correctly):

ns_with_re_split(elms + mixed) = ['alm5', 'elm0', 'elm1', 'Elm2', 'elm9', 'elm10', 'Elm11', 'Elm12', 'elm13', 'elm99', 'zlm1']
ns_with_re_split(ipv4s) = ['10.0.0.2', '10.0.0.5', '10.0.0.20', '192.168.0.2', '192.168.0.4', '192.168.0.12']

Q: How to mix css3 transform properties without overriding (in realtime)? A:

This is an old question, but it's a high Google result when searching for "css transform additive" so I wanted to add a modern answer. This will work when you want to animate a CSS transform.

animation-composition: add

Apply this to the styles for an element being animated and any transform properties applied in the animation will be added to any existing ones.

https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/CSS/Reference/Properties/animation-composition

Q: Installing NPAPI plugin for google chrome and mozilla firefox A:

In FireFox, place your plugin in the FireFox installation folder under a new/existing folder called "plugins", then restart FireFox and it should then be read to use.

Google Chrome does not support ActiveX and neither does FireFox. If you need to do advanced functionality, use your plugin.

For Google Chrome, try placing the plugin file in the installation folder or a folder called "Extensions" in the installation folder and then restart the browser.

Hope this helps.

Q: Implementing the double-click event on Silverlight 4 Datagrid A:

First, Button.Command is not for double-click. It will work with single click as well.

You need to change like that. ElementName=dgUserRoles, Path=DataContext.

 Command="{Binding ElementName=dgUserRoles, Path=DataContext.EditRoleClickedCommand}"
